title: The Montgomery bus boycott, 1955–1956
stem:
The following sources are original practice texts written for this question.

Source A: Extract from a fictional letter by a Black domestic worker in Montgomery to her sister, January 1956.
"Every morning I walk the four miles to the house where I work and four miles home. My feet ache, but I would rather walk in dignity than ride in shame. The church car pool picks me up when it rains. Mrs White says she will drive me herself if I keep quiet about it."

Source B: Extract from a fictional statement by a Montgomery city commissioner to local newspapers, February 1956.
"The so-called boycott is the work of outside agitators and a handful of ministers who are breaking state law against conspiracy to hinder business. The bus company is losing money and law-abiding citizens of both races are suffering. The city will not surrender its laws to intimidation."

Source C: Extract from a fictional textbook for university students, 2008.
"The boycott's success rested on two foundations. Local organisations, especially the Women's Political Council, had prepared the ground long before Rosa Parks' arrest, and the church network sustained a car pool for over a year. Yet it was the federal courts, in Browder v. Gayle, that finally forced the city to integrate its buses."

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: According to Source C, why was the Montgomery bus boycott successful?
markscheme: local organisations such as the Women's Political Council had prepared beforehand
the church network sustained it
a car pool kept it going for over a year
the federal courts (Browder v. Gayle) forced integration

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What does Source A suggest about the commitment of ordinary participants in the boycott?
markscheme: participants endured hardship / walked long distances
they valued dignity over convenience
the community organised support such as car pools
some white employers quietly helped

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source B for a historian studying opposition to the boycott.
markscheme: Value (origin): a city commissioner speaking at the time reveals the official view of local authorities
Value (purpose): intended to discredit the boycott publicly, so it shows the arguments and legal tactics used against it (conspiracy laws)
Value (content): shows economic impact on the bus company and the claim of 'outside agitators'
Limitation (purpose): a public statement designed to persuade; likely to exaggerate and to deny local Black support
Limitation (content): does not reveal private views, violence or the role of groups such as White Citizens' Councils
parts.notes: Maximum 3 if only value or only limitations are addressed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast what Sources A and B reveal about the Montgomery bus boycott.
markscheme: Similarity: both show the boycott was sustained and widespread enough to have an impact
Similarity: both suggest hardship / suffering for people in Montgomery
Difference: A presents the boycott as a local, grassroots and dignified choice; B blames outside agitators and ministers
Difference: A sees the boycott as a moral stand; B presents it as illegal conspiracy
Difference: A shows some white sympathy (the employer); B claims both races suffer and implies unity against the boycott
Difference: A focuses on individual sacrifice; B focuses on economic losses to the bus company
parts.notes: Reward linked, running comparison. End-on description: maximum 3.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent was the Montgomery bus boycott a success for the civil rights movement?
markscheme: Clear judgement on 'to what extent', weighing success and limitations
Achieved bus desegregation in Montgomery in December 1956 after Browder v. Gayle (Source C)
Demonstrated the power of mass non-violent direct action and community organisation (Sources A, C)
Brought Martin Luther King Jr to national prominence and led to the founding of the SCLC (1957)
Economic pressure on the bus company (Source B)
Limitations: legal victory came from the courts, not the boycott alone (Source C)
Limitations: little change to other segregation or voting rights; violence followed (e.g. bombings of churches and homes)
Limitations: massive resistance continued across the South (Source B's defiance)
Integration of sources with accurate own knowledge throughout
parts.notes: Top band (7–9): focused, balanced argument integrating sources and own knowledge with a clear conclusion.
